meta.topic: PDE 解法与理论：达朗贝尔、傅里叶级数法、Sturm–Liouville、格林函数、Dirichlet/Neumann、最大值原理、适定性

zh: 设 $a>0$，$u\in C^2(\mathbb{R}\times[0,\infty))$ 解 $u_{tt}=a^2u_{xx}$。作特征坐标 $\xi=x-at$、$\eta=x+at$。由链式法则，$$\begin{aligned}u_{tt}-a^2u_{xx}&=u_{\xi\xi}(-a)^2+2u_{\xi\eta}(-a)(a)+u_{\eta\eta}a^2\\&\quad-a^2(u_{\xi\xi}+2u_{\xi\eta}+u_{\eta\eta})=-4a^2u_{\xi\eta}.\end{aligned}$$ 因此方程等价于 $u_{\xi\eta}=0$。由 $u_{\xi\eta}=0$ 知 $u_\xi$ 与 $\eta$ 无关，故 $u_\xi=f(\xi)$；再对 $\xi$ 积分得 $$u=F(\xi)+G(\eta)=F(x-at)+G(x+at),$$ 其中 $F,G\in C^2$。反之，任意这样的 $F,G$ 代入都给出解，所以这是 $C^2$ 通解。
令 $t=0$，由初始位移条件 $u(x,0)=\varphi(x)$ 得 $$F(x)+G(x)=\varphi(x)\qquad(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}).$$ 这是一条关于 $F,G$ 的方程，只确定它们的和；要分离出 $F$ 与 $G$，还需要初始速度提供的第二条方程。

对 $t$ 求导：$$u_t(x,t)=-aF'(x-at)+aG'(x+at).$$ 令 $t=0$ 并用 $u_t(x,0)=\psi(x)$，得 $-aF'(x)+aG'(x)=\psi(x)$。从 $x_0$ 到 $x$ 积分：$$-a[F(x)-F(x_0)]+a[G(x)-G(x_0)]=\int_{x_0}^{x}\psi(s)\,ds.$$ 令 $A=F-G$，则 $A'=-\psi/a$，故 $$\begin{aligned}F&=\frac{\varphi}{2}-\frac{1}{2a}\int_{x_0}^{x}\psi+\frac{C}{2},\\ G&=\frac{\varphi}{2}+\frac{1}{2a}\int_{x_0}^{x}\psi-\frac{C}{2}.\end{aligned}$$ 这里 $C$ 是积分常数；代入 $F(x-at)+G(x+at)$ 时两个 $C/2$ 相消，只剩 $$\begin{aligned}u(x,t)&=\frac12[\varphi(x-at)+\varphi(x+at)]\\&\quad+\frac{1}{2a}\int_{x-at}^{x+at}\psi(s)\,ds.\end{aligned}$$ 系数 $\frac12$ 来自解 $F+G=\varphi$，$\frac{1}{2a}$ 来自对速度积分；积分区间端点正是 $x\pm at$，区间长度为 $2at$。

直接验证。$t=0$ 时第二项积分为零，第一项为 $\frac12[\varphi(x)+\varphi(x)]=\varphi(x)$。对 $t$ 求导：$$u_t=\frac a2[\varphi'(x+at)-\varphi'(x-at)]+\frac12[\psi(x+at)+\psi(x-at)],$$ 故 $u_t(x,0)=\frac12[\psi(x)+\psi(x)]=\psi(x)$。再求导并与 $u_{xx}$ 比较：若 $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb{R})$、$\psi\in C^1(\mathbb{R})$，则 $$\begin{aligned}u_{tt}&=a^2\Big\{\frac12[\varphi''(x+at)+\varphi''(x-at)]\\&\quad+\frac{1}{2a}[\psi'(x+at)-\psi'(x-at)]\Big\}=a^2u_{xx}.\end{aligned}$$ 所以公式在所述 $C^2/C^1$ 条件下给出经典解；数据更弱时公式仍可定义广义解，但不能直接作二阶逐项求导。

公式读出依赖区间：$u(x,t)$ 只用到 $\varphi$ 在 $x-at$ 与 $x+at$ 两点的值，以及 $\psi$ 在 $[x-at,x+at]$ 上的值。若在 $t=0$ 只改变该区间外的初值，$u(x,t)$ 不变；反之，位于 $x_0$ 的初值扰动在时刻 $t$ 最多影响到 $[x_0-at,x_0+at]$。这给出有限传播速度 $a$ 与因果性：$t$ 时刻的解只由过去光锥内的数据决定。区间长度 $2at$ 也解释了第二项为何除以 $2a$：它把区间上的速度贡献换算成位移。

全直线公式不能直接用于半直线或有限区间，边界条件要靠延拓实现。对 $x>0$ 的 Dirichlet 条件 $u(0,t)=0$，把 $\varphi,\psi$ 奇延拓到 $\mathbb R$：$\tilde\varphi(-x)=-\varphi(x)$、$\tilde\psi(-x)=-\psi(x)$，则 $\tilde u(0,t)=0$，限制回 $x\ge0$ 即为解。要得到 $C^2$ 经典解，除 $\varphi\in C^2$、$\psi\in C^1$ 外还需角点相容性 $\varphi(0)=0$、$\psi(0)=0$、$\varphi''(0)=0$；否则奇延拓在 $0$ 处不是 $C^2$，解可能出现角点奇性。Neumann 条件 $u_x(0,t)=0$ 改用偶延拓，需 $\varphi'(0)=0$、$\psi'(0)=0$ 才能保持 $C^2$；有限区间 $[0,L]$ 则在两端同时作镜像延拓，并须满足两端相应的相容性。非齐次边界先取满足边界条件的特解齐次化，再套公式。
en: Let $a>0$ and let $u\in C^2(\mathbb{R}\times[0,\infty))$ solve $u_{tt}=a^2u_{xx}$. Introduce the characteristic coordinates $\xi=x-at$ and $\eta=x+at$. The chain rule gives $$\begin{aligned}u_{tt}-a^2u_{xx}&=u_{\xi\xi}(-a)^2+2u_{\xi\eta}(-a)(a)+u_{\eta\eta}a^2\\&\quad-a^2(u_{\xi\xi}+2u_{\xi\eta}+u_{\eta\eta})=-4a^2u_{\xi\eta}.\end{aligned}$$ Hence the PDE is equivalent to $u_{\xi\eta}=0$. Since $u_{\xi\eta}=0$, $u_\xi$ is independent of $\eta$, so $u_\xi=f(\xi)$; integrating in $\xi$ then gives $$u=F(\xi)+G(\eta)=F(x-at)+G(x+at),$$ with $F,G\in C^2$. Conversely, every such pair $F,G$ gives a solution, so this is the general $C^2$ solution.

Setting $t=0$ and imposing the initial displacement $u(x,0)=\varphi(x)$ yields $$F(x)+G(x)=\varphi(x)\qquad(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}).$$ This is a single equation for $F$ and $G$; it determines only their sum. The second equation needed to separate $F$ from $G$ comes from the initial velocity.

Differentiating in $t$ gives $$u_t(x,t)=-aF'(x-at)+aG'(x+at).$$ At $t=0$, the condition $u_t(x,0)=\psi(x)$ yields $-aF'(x)+aG'(x)=\psi(x)$. Integrating from $x_0$ to $x$, $$-a[F(x)-F(x_0)]+a[G(x)-G(x_0)]=\int_{x_0}^{x}\psi(s)\,ds.$$ With $A=F-G$ we have $A'=-\psi/a$, hence $$\begin{aligned}F&=\frac{\varphi}{2}-\frac{1}{2a}\int_{x_0}^{x}\psi+\frac{C}{2},\\ G&=\frac{\varphi}{2}+\frac{1}{2a}\int_{x_0}^{x}\psi-\frac{C}{2}.\end{aligned}$$ The constant $C$ cancels when $F(x-at)+G(x+at)$ is formed, leaving $$\begin{aligned}u(x,t)&=\frac12[\varphi(x-at)+\varphi(x+at)]\\&\quad+\frac{1}{2a}\int_{x-at}^{x+at}\psi(s)\,ds.\end{aligned}$$ The factor $\frac12$ comes from solving $F+G=\varphi$, and $\frac{1}{2a}$ from integrating the velocity; the endpoints are $x\pm at$ and the interval has length $2at$.

Direct verification. At $t=0$ the integral vanishes and the first term equals $\frac12[\varphi(x)+\varphi(x)]=\varphi(x)$. Differentiating in $t$, $$u_t=\frac a2[\varphi'(x+at)-\varphi'(x-at)]+\frac12[\psi(x+at)+\psi(x-at)],$$ so $u_t(x,0)=\frac12[\psi(x)+\psi(x)]=\psi(x)$. Differentiating once more and comparing with $u_{xx}$, for $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb{R})$ and $\psi\in C^1(\mathbb{R})$ we get $$\begin{aligned}u_{tt}&=a^2\Big\{\frac12[\varphi''(x+at)+\varphi''(x-at)]\\&\quad+\frac{1}{2a}[\psi'(x+at)-\psi'(x-at)]\Big\}=a^2u_{xx}.\end{aligned}$$ Thus the formula gives a classical solution under these $C^2/C^1$ hypotheses. For weaker data it still defines a generalized solution, but termwise second derivatives are no longer justified.

The formula exhibits the interval of dependence: $u(x,t)$ uses only $\varphi$ at the two points $x-at$ and $x+at$, and $\psi$ on $[x-at,x+at]$. Changing initial data outside this interval at $t=0$ leaves $u(x,t)$ unchanged; conversely, a disturbance initially at $x_0$ can influence at time $t$ only the interval $[x_0-at,x_0+at]$. This is finite propagation speed $a$ and causality: the solution at time $t$ is determined by data in the past light cone. The length $2at$ also explains the factor $\frac{1}{2a}$: it converts the velocity contribution over the interval into a displacement.

The whole-line formula cannot be applied directly on a half-line or a finite interval; boundary conditions are enforced by extension. For the Dirichlet condition $u(0,t)=0$ on $x>0$, extend $\varphi,\psi$ oddly to $\mathbb R$: $\tilde\varphi(-x)=-\varphi(x)$, $\tilde\psi(-x)=-\psi(x)$. Then $\tilde u(0,t)=0$, and its restriction to $x\ge0$ is the solution. A $C^2$ classical solution requires, besides $\varphi\in C^2$ and $\psi\in C^1$, the corner compatibility conditions $\varphi(0)=0$, $\psi(0)=0$, $\varphi''(0)=0$; otherwise the odd extension fails to be $C^2$ at $0$ and a corner singularity may appear. For the Neumann condition $u_x(0,t)=0$, use even extensions and require $\varphi'(0)=0$, $\psi'(0)=0$ to preserve $C^2$. On a finite interval $[0,L]$, reflect at both endpoints and impose the corresponding compatibility conditions at both ends. For nonhomogeneous boundary data, first subtract a particular solution satisfying the boundary conditions, then apply the formula.

zh: 先看齐次 Dirichlet 边界。设 $u$ 在 $0<x<L$、$t>0$ 上解热方程 $u_t=a^2u_{xx}$ 或波动方程 $u_{tt}=a^2u_{xx}$，且 $u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0$。令 $u=X(x)T(t)$，代入并除以 $a^2XT$：热方程给出 $X''/X=T'/(a^2T)$，波动方程给出 $X''/X=T''/(a^2T)$。左端只依赖 $x$、右端只依赖 $t$，故等于常数 $-\lambda$。于是 $$X''+\lambda X=0,\qquad X(0)=X(L)=0.$$ 若 $\lambda\le0$，通解为线性函数（$\lambda=0$）或双曲函数（$\lambda<0$），两个端点条件迫使 $X\equiv0$，得不到非平凡解。因此 $\lambda>0$，记 $\lambda=\mu^2$，则 $X=A\cos\mu x+B\sin\mu x$；$X(0)=0$ 给 $A=0$，$X(L)=0$ 给 $\sin\mu L=0$，故 $$\lambda_n=\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}\right)^2,\qquad X_n(x)=\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L},\quad n=1,2,\dots.$$ 特征值由边界条件决定，这是 $p=\rho=1$、$q=0$ 的 Sturm–Liouville 问题。

特征函数正交：$$\int_0^L\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\sin\frac{m\pi x}{L}\,dx=\frac L2\delta_{mn}.$$ 若解可写成 $u=\sum_{n\ge1}T_n(t)\sin(n\pi x/L)$ 且逐项积分合法，乘以 $\sin(m\pi x/L)$ 后积分，右端只剩 $n=m$ 项，得 $$T_n(t)=\frac2L\int_0^L u(x,t)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx.$$ 特别在 $t=0$：$$\begin{aligned}b_n&=\frac2L\int_0^L\varphi(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx,\\ \psi_n&=\frac2L\int_0^L\psi(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx.\end{aligned}$$ 这就是把初值投影到第 $n$ 个特征方向；$\sin(n\pi x/L)$ 在 $L^2(0,L)$ 中完备，故任何 $\varphi\in L^2$ 都有 $L^2$ 收敛的展开，但逐点或一致收敛还要看光滑性与相容性。

对热方程，代入级数并用正交性比较系数，得 $$T_n'+a^2\lambda_nT_n=0,\qquad T_n(0)=b_n,$$ 故 $$T_n(t)=b_n e^{-a^2\lambda_nt}=b_n e^{-(n\pi a/L)^2t}.$$ 于是 $$u(x,t)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n e^{-(n\pi a/L)^2t}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}.$$ 每个模式独立衰减，衰减率 $\lambda_na^2=(n\pi a/L)^2$ 随 $n^2$ 增长，高频分量被极快抹平。对 $t\ge\delta>0$，$e^{-(n\pi a/L)^2t}\le e^{-(n\pi a/L)^2\delta}$，而 $e^{-cn^2\delta}$ 压过任意 $n^k$，故级数及其任意阶逐项导数一致收敛，$u\in C^\infty$；即使 $\varphi$ 仅属于 $L^2$，$t>0$ 后也光滑。若 $\varphi$ 连续并要求 $u$ 连续到 $t=0$，还需 $\varphi(0)=\varphi(L)=0$，否则正弦级数在端点收敛到 $0$ 而不是 $\varphi$ 的端点值。

对波动方程，$$T_n''+a^2\lambda_nT_n=0,\qquad \omega_n=a\sqrt{\lambda_n}=\frac{n\pi a}{L}.$$ 初始条件为 $T_n(0)=b_n$、$T_n'(0)=\psi_n$，故 $$T_n(t)=b_n\cos\omega_nt+\frac{\psi_n}{\omega_n}\sin\omega_nt.$$ 记 $$c_n=\frac{\psi_n}{\omega_n}=\frac{2}{n\pi a}\int_0^L\psi(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}dx,$$ 则 $$\begin{aligned}u(x,t)&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\Big[b_n\cos\frac{n\pi at}{L}\\&\quad+c_n\sin\frac{n\pi at}{L}\Big]\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}.\end{aligned}$$ 在 $t=0$ 时 $u=\sum b_n\sin(n\pi x/L)=\varphi$、$u_t=\sum\psi_n\sin(n\pi x/L)=\psi$（在相应收敛意义下）。每个模式只振荡、不衰减，角频率是 $n\pi a/L$，不是 $n\pi/L$。

逐项求导不是无条件成立。波动方程级数要作两次空间或时间求导；若系数满足 $$\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^2(|b_n|+|c_n|)<\infty,$$ 则二阶逐项导数绝对且一致收敛，因为 $\omega_n^2$ 与 $n^2$ 同阶。一个可核对的充分条件是 $\varphi\in C^4$、$\psi\in C^3$，且 $$\varphi(0)=\varphi(L)=\varphi''(0)=\varphi''(L)=0,\quad \psi(0)=\psi(L)=\psi''(0)=\psi''(L)=0.$$ 对 $\psi$ 分部积分三次、对 $\varphi$ 四次，可得 $b_n=O(n^{-4})$、$\psi_n=O(n^{-3})$，从而 $c_n=\psi_n/\omega_n=O(n^{-4})$，上述级数绝对收敛，逐项二阶导数一致收敛。若数据只有 $C^2/C^1$，达朗贝尔公式仍可能给出经典解，但傅里叶级数未必能逐项求导两次；分段光滑数据在跳跃处出现 Gibbs 振荡，级数在跳跃点收敛到左右极限的平均值。

非齐次源项 $f(x,t)=\sum f_n(t)\sin(n\pi x/L)$ 把系数方程变成 $$\begin{aligned}T_n''+\omega_n^2T_n&=f_n(t)\quad(\text{波动}),\\ T_n'+a^2\lambda_nT_n&=f_n(t)\quad(\text{热}).\end{aligned}$$ 对波动方程，若 $f_n(t)=A\cos\omega_nt$，即外力频率恰为第 $n$ 个固有频率，则 $$T_n(t)=\frac{A}{2\omega_n}t\sin\omega_nt+\text{齐次解}$$ 含长期项 $t\sin\omega_nt$，振幅随 $t$ 线性增长，这就是共振。若外力频率 $\Omega\ne\omega_n$，特解分母为 $\omega_n^2-\Omega^2$，有界；$\Omega$ 接近 $\omega_n$ 时振幅变大但仍有限（拍频），只有 $\Omega=\omega_n$ 且 $A\ne0$ 才出现长期项。热方程是一阶的，没有这种振荡共振；但若 $f_n(t)=Ae^{-a^2\lambda_nt}$ 与齐次衰减率相同，也会出现 $t e^{-a^2\lambda_nt}$ 的长期项。

边界条件还决定特征函数系。Neumann 条件 $u_x(0,t)=u_x(L,t)=0$ 给出 $X_n=\cos(n\pi x/L)$，$n=0,1,2,\dots$，其中 $n=0$ 对应 $\lambda_0=0$ 的常数模式；热方程中它不衰减，故解趋向初值的平均 $\frac1L\int_0^L\varphi$，而不是零。Robin 条件 $\alpha u+\beta u_x=0$ 给出更一般的 Sturm–Liouville 特征值，通常只能数值求解。非齐次边界（如 $u(0,t)=g_0(t)$、$u(L,t)=g_L(t)$）先作 $$U(x,t)=g_0(t)+\frac{x}{L}\bigl(g_L(t)-g_0(t)\bigr),$$ 令 $v=u-U$；$v$ 满足齐次边界，但方程右端多出 $-U_t+a^2U_{xx}$（热）或 $-U_{tt}+a^2U_{xx}$（波动）。初始数据还必须与边界条件在角点 $(0,0)$、$(L,0)$ 相容（如 Dirichlet 的 $\varphi(0)=g_0(0)$、$\psi(0)=g_0'(0)$，$x=L$ 端同理），否则古典解不可能在闭区域上连续，级数只给出广义解。
en: Begin with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. Let $u$ solve the heat equation $u_t=a^2u_{xx}$ or the wave equation $u_{tt}=a^2u_{xx}$ on $0<x<L$, $t>0$, with $u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0$. Put $u=X(x)T(t)$ and divide by $a^2XT$: the heat equation gives $X''/X=T'/(a^2T)$, and the wave equation gives $X''/X=T''/(a^2T)$. The left side depends only on $x$ and the right side only on $t$, so both equal a constant $-\lambda$. Thus $$X''+\lambda X=0,\qquad X(0)=X(L)=0.$$ If $\lambda\le0$, the general solution is linear ($\lambda=0$) or hyperbolic ($\lambda<0$), and the two endpoint conditions force $X\equiv0$, so no nontrivial solution arises. Hence $\lambda>0$; writing $\lambda=\mu^2$ gives $X=A\cos\mu x+B\sin\mu x$. The condition $X(0)=0$ forces $A=0$, and $X(L)=0$ forces $\sin\mu L=0$. Therefore $$\lambda_n=\left(\frac{n\pi}{L}\right)^2,\qquad X_n(x)=\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L},\quad n=1,2,\dots.$$ The eigenvalues are fixed by the boundary conditions; this is the Sturm–Liouville problem with $p=\rho=1$, $q=0$.

The eigenfunctions are orthogonal: $$\int_0^L\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\sin\frac{m\pi x}{L}\,dx=\frac L2\delta_{mn}.$$ If the solution can be written as $u=\sum_{n\ge1}T_n(t)\sin(n\pi x/L)$ and termwise integration is legitimate, multiplying by $\sin(m\pi x/L)$ and integrating leaves only the $n=m$ term: $$T_n(t)=\frac2L\int_0^L u(x,t)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx.$$ In particular, at $t=0$, $$\begin{aligned}b_n&=\frac2L\int_0^L\varphi(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx,\\ \psi_n&=\frac2L\int_0^L\psi(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\,dx.\end{aligned}$$ These are the projections of the initial data onto the $n$-th eigenfunction. Since $\sin(n\pi x/L)$ is complete in $L^2(0,L)$, every $\varphi\in L^2$ has an $L^2$-convergent expansion; pointwise or uniform convergence requires additional smoothness and compatibility.

For the heat equation, substituting the series and comparing coefficients via orthogonality gives $$T_n'+a^2\lambda_nT_n=0,\qquad T_n(0)=b_n,$$ hence $$T_n(t)=b_n e^{-a^2\lambda_nt}=b_n e^{-(n\pi a/L)^2t}.$$ Therefore $$u(x,t)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n e^{-(n\pi a/L)^2t}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}.$$ Each mode decays independently, with rate $\lambda_na^2=(n\pi a/L)^2$ growing like $n^2$, so high-frequency components are wiped out extremely fast. For $t\ge\delta>0$, $e^{-(n\pi a/L)^2t}\le e^{-(n\pi a/L)^2\delta}$, and $e^{-cn^2\delta}$ dominates every power $n^k$; hence the series and all its termwise derivatives converge uniformly and $u\in C^\infty$; even if $\varphi$ is merely in $L^2$, the solution is smooth for $t>0$. If $\varphi$ is continuous and $u$ is required to be continuous up to $t=0$, one also needs $\varphi(0)=\varphi(L)=0$; otherwise the sine series tends to $0$ at the endpoints rather than to the endpoint values of $\varphi$.

For the wave equation, $$T_n''+a^2\lambda_nT_n=0,\qquad \omega_n=a\sqrt{\lambda_n}=\frac{n\pi a}{L}.$$ The initial conditions are $T_n(0)=b_n$ and $T_n'(0)=\psi_n$, so $$T_n(t)=b_n\cos\omega_nt+\frac{\psi_n}{\omega_n}\sin\omega_nt.$$ Writing $$c_n=\frac{\psi_n}{\omega_n}=\frac{2}{n\pi a}\int_0^L\psi(x)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}dx,$$ we obtain $$\begin{aligned}u(x,t)&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\Big[b_n\cos\frac{n\pi at}{L}\\&\quad+c_n\sin\frac{n\pi at}{L}\Big]\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}.\end{aligned}$$ At $t=0$, $u=\sum b_n\sin(n\pi x/L)=\varphi$ and $u_t=\sum\psi_n\sin(n\pi x/L)=\psi$ in the appropriate convergence sense. Each mode oscillates without decay, with angular frequency $n\pi a/L$, not $n\pi/L$.

Termwise differentiation is not automatic. The wave series must be differentiated twice in space or time. If the coefficients satisfy $$\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^2(|b_n|+|c_n|)<\infty,$$ then the second termwise derivatives converge absolutely and uniformly, since $\omega_n^2$ is comparable to $n^2$. A checkable sufficient condition is $\varphi\in C^4$, $\psi\in C^3$, together with $$\varphi(0)=\varphi(L)=\varphi''(0)=\varphi''(L)=0,\quad \psi(0)=\psi(L)=\psi''(0)=\psi''(L)=0.$$ Integrating by parts three times for $\psi$ and four times for $\varphi$ gives $b_n=O(n^{-4})$ and $\psi_n=O(n^{-3})$, hence $c_n=\psi_n/\omega_n=O(n^{-4})$; the series above then converges absolutely and its second termwise derivatives converge uniformly. With only $C^2/C^1$ data, d'Alembert's formula may still give a classical solution, but the Fourier series need not be twice termwise differentiable. For piecewise smooth data, Gibbs oscillations appear at jumps, and the series converges at a jump to the average of the one-sided limits.

A source term $f(x,t)=\sum f_n(t)\sin(n\pi x/L)$ turns the coefficient equations into $$\begin{aligned}T_n''+\omega_n^2T_n&=f_n(t)\quad(\text{wave}),\\ T_n'+a^2\lambda_nT_n&=f_n(t)\quad(\text{heat}).\end{aligned}$$ For the wave equation, if $f_n(t)=A\cos\omega_nt$, so that the forcing frequency equals the $n$-th natural frequency, then $$T_n(t)=\frac{A}{2\omega_n}t\sin\omega_nt+\text{homogeneous solution}$$ contains the secular term $t\sin\omega_nt$, whose amplitude grows linearly in $t$; this is resonance. If the forcing frequency $\Omega\ne\omega_n$, the particular solution has denominator $\omega_n^2-\Omega^2$ and is bounded; as $\Omega$ approaches $\omega_n$ the amplitude becomes large but remains finite (beats), and a secular term occurs only when $\Omega=\omega_n$ and $A\ne0$. The heat equation is first order and has no oscillatory resonance of this kind; however, if $f_n(t)=Ae^{-a^2\lambda_nt}$ matches the homogeneous decay rate, a secular term $t e^{-a^2\lambda_nt}$ appears.

The boundary conditions also determine the eigenfunction system. Neumann conditions $u_x(0,t)=u_x(L,t)=0$ give $X_n=\cos(n\pi x/L)$, $n=0,1,2,\dots$, where $n=0$ corresponds to the constant mode with $\lambda_0=0$. In the heat equation this mode does not decay, so the solution tends to the initial average $\frac1L\int_0^L\varphi$ rather than to zero. Robin conditions $\alpha u+\beta u_x=0$ lead to a more general Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue problem, usually solved numerically. For nonhomogeneous boundary data such as $u(0,t)=g_0(t)$, $u(L,t)=g_L(t)$, first set $$U(x,t)=g_0(t)+\frac{x}{L}\bigl(g_L(t)-g_0(t)\bigr),$$ and let $v=u-U$. Then $v$ satisfies homogeneous boundary conditions, but the equation acquires the additional term $-U_t+a^2U_{xx}$ (heat) or $-U_{tt}+a^2U_{xx}$ (wave). The initial data must also be compatible with the boundary data at the corners $(0,0)$ and $(L,0)$ (for Dirichlet, $\varphi(0)=g_0(0)$ and $\psi(0)=g_0'(0)$, and similarly at $x=L$); otherwise a classical solution cannot be continuous on the closed region, and the series gives only a generalized solution.

zh: 设 $p\in C^1[a,b]$、$q,\rho\in C[a,b]$，且 $p(x)>0$、$\rho(x)>0$。施图姆–刘维尔方程写成自伴形式 $$(p(x)y')'+[\lambda\rho(x)-q(x)]y=0.$$ 令 $L[y]=(py')'-qy$，则方程即 $L[y]=-\lambda\rho y$。对两个 $C^2$ 函数 $y_m,y_n$ 直接求导可验证拉格朗日恒等式 $$y_mL[y_n]-y_nL[y_m]=\frac{d}{dx}\left[p(y_my_n'-y_ny_m')\right].$$ 右端是全导数，这是自伴性的微分形式：$L$ 关于无权内积 $\int_a^b fg\,dx$ 对称；等价地，$T=\frac1\rho L$ 关于带权内积 $\langle f,g\rangle_\rho=\int_a^b\rho fg\,dx$ 对称。积分后唯一的障碍是边界项。

设边界条件为分离型：$$\begin{aligned}\alpha y(a)+\beta y'(a)&=0,\\ \gamma y(b)+\delta y'(b)&=0.\end{aligned}$$ 其中 $\alpha,\beta$ 不同时为零，$\gamma,\delta$ 不同时为零，系数取实数。若 $y_m,y_n$ 都满足同一端的条件，则该端的两个向量 $(y,y')$ 同属于一条过原点的直线，行列式 $y_my_n'-y_ny_m'$ 为零，故 $$p(y_my_n'-y_ny_m')\Big|_a^b=0.$$ 把拉格朗日恒等式在 $[a,b]$ 上积分，并使用 $L[y_k]=-\lambda_k\rho y_k$，得 $$(\lambda_m-\lambda_n)\int_a^b\rho y_my_n\,dx=0.$$ 若 $\lambda_m\ne\lambda_n$，立即得到带权正交。

特征值全为实数。若允许复值函数，设 $y$ 是特征值 $\lambda$ 的特征函数，用 $\bar y$ 乘方程 $L[y]=-\lambda\rho y$ 并积分：$$\int_a^b[(py')'\bar y-q|y|^2]dx=-\lambda\int_a^b\rho|y|^2dx.$$ 对第一项分部积分得 $$\int_a^b p|y'|^2dx+\int_a^b q|y|^2dx-\big[p y'\bar y\big]_a^b=\lambda\int_a^b\rho|y|^2dx.$$ 在分离型实系数边界条件下，边界项 $p y'\bar y$ 是实数（Dirichlet/Neumann 时为零，Robin 时由 $y'=-\alpha y/\beta$ 化为实数），且分母 $\int\rho|y|^2>0$，故 $\lambda$ 等于一个实数，特征值必实。

u^2/x$ 的正交性是 $\int_0^R xJ_

完备性与展开：正则 SL 问题（有限区间、$p>0,\rho>0$、系数连续、分离边界）的特征值可排成 $$\lambda_1<\lambda_2<\cdots\to\infty,$$ 对应的特征函数 $\{y_n\}$ 在 $L^2_\rho(a,b)$ 中完备。于是任意 $f\in L^2_\rho$ 可展开为 $$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_ny_n(x),\\ f_n&=\frac{\langle f,y_n\rangle_\rho}{\|y_n\|_\rho^2}=\frac{\int_a^b\rho f y_n}{\int_a^b\rho y_n^2},\end{aligned}$$ 级数在 $L^2_\rho$ 意义下收敛。若 $f$ 更光滑并满足边界相容性，则收敛可以是一致的，且可逐项求导；仅有 $L^2$ 时不能把逐点等式或逐项求导当成结论。奇异问题（$p$ 在端点为零或区间无界）需要额外条件（如端点有界性、limit-point/limit-circle），Legendre、Bessel 的完备性在这些条件下仍成立。

瑞利商与特征值排序：Dirichlet 或 Neumann 边界时边界项为零；用 $y$ 乘方程并积分，得 $$\lambda=\frac{\int_a^b\left[p(x)(y')^2+q(x)y^2\right]dx}{\int_a^b\rho(x)y^2dx}.$$ 对一般 Robin 边界，必须保留边界项：$$\lambda=\frac{\int_a^b\left[p(y')^2+q y^2\right]dx-\bigl[p y y'\bigr]_a^b}{\int_a^b\rho y^2dx}.$$ 因此，在 $p>0$、$q\ge0$ 且公式中的边界项 $-\bigl[p y y'\bigr]_a^b$ 非负时，可推出 $\lambda\ge0$（这些是充分条件，$q\ge0$ 不是必要条件）。在满足边界条件的函数类中，这个商的最小值就是 $\lambda_1$，最小值点是对应特征函数；后续特征值由在 $\langle\cdot,y_1\rangle_\rho=\cdots=0$ 的子空间上取最小值得出（Courant–Fischer 极小极大原理）。这也说明 $\lambda_1$ 单重且特征函数可取定号（Sturm 振荡定理）。在系数足够光滑时，任何二阶线性方程 $a y''+b y'+c y+\lambda d y=0$（$a>0$）乘以 $\frac1a e^{\int b/a}$ 都可化为 SL 形式，其中 $p=e^{\int b/a}$、$\rho=pd/a$、$q=-pc/a$；若原方程首项系数 $a$ 在端点退化或区间无界，则问题是奇异的，不能直接套用正则问题的全部结论。
en: Let $p\in C^1[a,b]$ and $q,\rho\in C[a,b]$, with $p(x)>0$ and $\rho(x)>0$. The Sturm–Liouville equation is written in self-adjoint form $$(p(x)y')'+[\lambda\rho(x)-q(x)]y=0.$$ Setting $L[y]=(py')'-qy$, the equation becomes $L[y]=-\lambda\rho y$. A direct differentiation for two $C^2$ functions $y_m,y_n$ verifies Lagrange's identity $$y_mL[y_n]-y_nL[y_m]=\frac{d}{dx}\left[p(y_my_n'-y_ny_m')\right].$$ The right side is a total derivative; this is the differential form of self-adjointness. The operator $L$ is symmetric for the unweighted inner product $\int_a^b fg\,dx$; equivalently, $T=\frac1\rho L$ is symmetric for the weighted inner product $\langle f,g\rangle_\rho=\int_a^b\rho fg\,dx$. After integration the only obstruction is the boundary term.

Take separated boundary conditions $$ egin{aligned}\alpha y(a)+ eta y'(a)&=0,\ \gamma y(b)+\delta y'(b)&=0.\end{aligned}$$ where $(\alpha, eta)
e(0,0)$ and $(\gamma,\delta)
e(0,0)$, with real coefficients. If $y_m,y_n$ both satisfy the condition at one endpoint, the two vectors $(y,y')$ at that endpoint lie on the same line through the origin, so the determinant $y_my_n'-y_ny_m'$ vanishes there. Hence $$p(y_my_n'-y_ny_m')\Big|_a^b=0.$$ Integrating Lagrange's identity over $[a,b]$ and using $L[y_k]=-\lambda_kho y_k$ gives $$(\lambda_m-\lambda_n)\int_a^bho y_my_n\,dx=0.$$ If $\lambda_m
e\lambda_n$, weighted orthogonality follows immediately.

All eigenvalues are real. Allowing complex-valued functions, let $y$ be an eigenfunction with eigenvalue $\lambda$ and multiply $L[y]=-\lambda\rho y$ by $\bar y$, then integrate: $$\int_a^b[(py')'\bar y-q|y|^2]dx=-\lambda\int_a^b\rho|y|^2dx.$$ Integrating the first term by parts gives $$\int_a^b p|y'|^2dx+\int_a^b q|y|^2dx-\big[p y'\bar y\big]_a^b=\lambda\int_a^b\rho|y|^2dx.$$ For separated boundary conditions with real coefficients the boundary term $p y'\bar y$ is real (it vanishes for Dirichlet or Neumann, and for Robin $y'=-\alpha y/\beta$ makes it real). Since $\int\rho|y|^2>0$, the quotient is real; hence every eigenvalue is real.

Orthogonality and the weight. If $\lambda_m
e\lambda_n$, then $$\int_a^bho(x)y_m(x)y_n(x)\,dx=0.$$ The weight $ho$ cannot be dropped: for Bessel's equation $p=x$, $ho=x$, $q=
u^2/x$, orthogonality reads $\int_0^R xJ_
u(\mu_mx)J_
u(\mu_nx)dx=0$, not an unweighted integral. If a repeated eigenvalue occurs (for example under periodic boundary conditions), eigenfunctions belonging to the same eigenvalue are orthonormalized by Gram–Schmidt; for a regular problem with separated boundary conditions every eigenvalue is simple, so this step is unnecessary. For $-y''=\lambda y$ with $y(0)=y(L)=0$, $p=ho=1$ and the eigenfunctions $\sin(n\pi x/L)$ are orthogonal. Legendre's equation $p=1-x^2$, $ho=1$ on $[-1,1]$ gives orthogonality of the $P_n$, but $p$ vanishes at the endpoints, so this is a singular problem.

Completeness and expansion. For a regular Sturm–Liouville problem (finite interval, $p>0$, $\rho>0$, continuous coefficients, separated boundary conditions), the eigenvalues can be ordered as $$\lambda_1<\lambda_2<\cdots\to\infty,$$ and the corresponding eigenfunctions $\{y_n\}$ form a complete system in $L^2_\rho(a,b)$. Thus every $f\in L^2_\rho$ expands as $$\begin{aligned}f(x)&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_ny_n(x),\\ f_n&=\frac{\langle f,y_n\rangle_\rho}{\|y_n\|_\rho^2}=\frac{\int_a^b\rho f y_n}{\int_a^b\rho y_n^2},\end{aligned}$$ with convergence in $L^2_\rho$. If $f$ is smoother and satisfies the boundary compatibility conditions, the convergence can be uniform and termwise differentiation is permitted; with only $L^2$ data, neither pointwise equality nor termwise differentiation is justified. Singular problems ($p$ vanishing at an endpoint, or an unbounded interval) require extra conditions such as boundedness at the endpoint or limit-point/limit-circle alternatives; completeness for Legendre and Bessel systems still holds under those conditions.

The Rayleigh quotient and ordering of eigenvalues. For Dirichlet or Neumann boundary conditions the boundary term vanishes; multiplying the equation by $y$ and integrating gives $$\lambda=\frac{\int_a^b\left[p(x)(y')^2+q(x)y^2\right]dx}{\int_a^b\rho(x)y^2dx}.$$ For general Robin boundary conditions, the boundary term must be retained: $$\lambda=\frac{\int_a^b\left[p(y')^2+q y^2\right]dx-\bigl[p y y'\bigr]_a^b}{\int_a^b\rho y^2dx}.$$ Thus, if $p>0$, $q\ge0$ and the boundary term $-\bigl[p y y'\bigr]_a^b$ in the formula is nonnegative, then $\lambda\ge0$ follows (these are sufficient conditions; $q\ge0$ is not necessary). Over the class of functions satisfying the boundary conditions, the minimum of this quotient is $\lambda_1$, attained at the first eigenfunction; subsequent eigenvalues are obtained by minimizing over the subspaces $\langle\cdot,y_1\rangle_\rho=\cdots=0$ (the Courant–Fischer min–max principle). This also shows that $\lambda_1$ is simple and its eigenfunction can be chosen of one sign (Sturm's oscillation theorem). For sufficiently smooth coefficients, every second-order linear equation $a y''+b y'+c y+\lambda d y=0$ with $a>0$, after multiplication by $\frac1a e^{\int b/a}$, takes Sturm–Liouville form with $p=e^{\int b/a}$, $\rho=pd/a$, $q=-pc/a$. If the leading coefficient $a$ degenerates at an endpoint, or the interval is unbounded, the problem is singular and not all conclusions for the regular case apply.

zh: 设 $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ 有界、边界光滑，考虑 $-\Delta$ 配齐次 Dirichlet 条件。格林函数 $G(x,\xi)$ 定义为分布意义下 $$\begin{aligned}-\Delta_xG(x,\xi)&=\delta(x-\xi),\qquad x\in\Omega,\\ G(x,\xi)&=0,\qquad x\in\partial\Omega.\end{aligned}$$ 对任意测试函数 $\eta$，这等价于 $\int_\Omega G(x,\xi)(-\Delta\eta(x))dx=\eta(\xi)$。在 $\Omega\setminus\{\xi\}$ 内 $G$ 调和；在 $x=\xi$ 处出现基本解的奇性，一维表现为导数跳变，高维表现为 $-\nabla G$ 围绕 $\xi$ 的通量为 $1$。一维 $(0,1)$ 上可直接解出 $$G(x,\xi)=\begin{cases}x(1-\xi),&0\le x\le\xi,\\ \xi(1-x),&\xi\le x\le1.\end{cases}$$ 它在 $x=\xi$ 连续、峰值为 $\xi(1-\xi)$，左右斜率分别为 $1-\xi$ 与 $-\xi$，跳变 $G'(\xi^+)-G'(\xi^-)=-1$，正好对应 $-G''=\delta$。

表示公式。设 $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^1(\bar\Omega)$ 解 $-\Delta u=f$、$u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$。在 $\Omega\setminus B_\varepsilon(\xi)$ 上对 $u$ 与 $G(\cdot,\xi)$ 用格林第二恒等式，再令 $\varepsilon\to0$（内边界 $\partial B_\varepsilon(\xi)$ 上的项收敛到 $-u(\xi)$，外边界就是 $\partial\Omega$）：$$\begin{aligned}\int_\Omega&(u\Delta G-G\Delta u)\,dx\\&=\int_{\partial\Omega}\left(u\frac{\partial G}{\partial n}-G\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\right)dS.\end{aligned}$$ 代入 $\Delta G=-\delta_\xi$、$\Delta u=-f$，左端为 $-u(\xi)+\int_\Omega Gf$；右端因 $G|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ 剩下 $\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,\partial_nG\,dS$。因此 $$\begin{aligned}u(\xi)&=\int_\Omega G(x,\xi)f(x)\,dx\\&\quad-\int_{\partial\Omega}g(x)\frac{\partial G}{\partial n_x}(x,\xi)\,dS_x.\end{aligned}$$ 当 $g=0$ 时就是 $u(\xi)=\int_\Omega Gf$：把 $f$ 看成点源的连续叠加，$G$ 是单位点源的响应。这里 $\partial_n$ 是外法向导数；换法向或把 $-\Delta$ 写成 $\Delta$ 都会改变边界项的符号。

对称性。对固定的 $x,\xi$，把格林第二恒等式用于 $G(\cdot,x)$ 与 $G(\cdot,\xi)$；两者都在边界为零，边界项消失，而 $-\Delta G(\cdot,x)=\delta_x$、$-\Delta G(\cdot,\xi)=\delta_\xi$，故 $$0=\int_\Omega\big[G(\eta,x)\Delta G(\eta,\xi)-G(\eta,\xi)\Delta G(\eta,x)\big]d\eta=-G(\xi,x)+G(x,\xi).$$ 于是 $G(x,\xi)=G(\xi,x)$：交换源点与观测点，响应不变。这是算子自伴且两端使用同一组自伴边界条件的直接推论；若算子含一阶项或边界条件不是自伴的，一般要用伴随问题的格林函数，对称性不成立。

基本解与符号约定。自由空间中 $-\Delta\Phi=\delta$ 的基本解为 $$\Phi(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{(n-2)\sigma_n}|x|^{2-n},&n\ge3,\\[2mm] -\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\log|x|=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\log\dfrac{1}{|x|},&n=2,\\[2mm] -\dfrac{|x|}{2},&n=1,\end{cases}$$ 其中 $\sigma_n$ 是单位球面面积（$\sigma_3=4\pi$）。三维即 $\Phi=1/(4\pi|x|)$；二维常写成 $\frac1{2\pi}\log\frac1{|x|}$。若把方程约定为 $\Delta\Phi=\delta$，二维要改成 $+\frac1{2\pi}\log|x|$，三维改成 $-\frac1{4\pi|x|}$。符号随约定而变，二维对数项尤其容易出错；基本解再加上任意调和函数仍是同一方程的基本解，边界条件才把它固定成格林函数。

有界区域上的构造。令 $G(x,\xi)=\Phi(x-\xi)-h(x,\xi)$，其中 $h(\cdot,\xi)$ 在 $\Omega$ 内调和，并在边界上取 $\Phi(x-\xi)$ 的边值。则 $-\Delta G=\delta_\xi$ 且 $G|_{\partial\Omega}=0$。对球 $B_R(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$ 与 $\xi\ne0$，用镜像法：取 $\xi^*=R^2\xi/|\xi|^2$，则 $$G(x,\xi)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\left[\frac{1}{|x-\xi|}-\frac{R}{|\xi|\,|x-\xi^*|}\right].$$ 当 $|x|=R$ 时，$|x-\xi^*|=\frac{R}{|\xi|}|x-\xi|$，故第二项与第一项相消，$G=0$；公式也对称。一般区域没有初等闭式，需解一个 Dirichlet 问题求 $h$；若边界只是 Lipschitz，$G$ 的存在与估计要更精细。齐次 Neumann 情形 $\partial_nG=0$ 不能直接这样定义：$-\Delta$ 在常数上有零特征值，$\delta$ 不满足 $\int_\Omega f=0$，必须去掉常数模式，改解 $-\Delta G=\delta-\frac1{|\Omega|}$；一般右端也只有满足 $\int_\Omega f=0$ 时才可解，且 $G$ 只能定义到相差一个常数（修正格林函数）。

特征函数展开与正性。设 $\{(\lambda_n,\varphi_n)\}$ 是 $-\Delta$ 配 Dirichlet 条件的标准正交特征系，$\lambda_n>0$，则 $$G(x,\xi)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{\varphi_n(x)\varphi_n(\xi)}{\lambda_n}.$$ 因为在分布意义下逐项作用 $-\Delta_x$ 得 $\sum\varphi_n(x)\varphi_n(\xi)=\delta(x-\xi)$，边界条件也逐项满足。对 $(0,1)$，$\varphi_n=\sqrt2\sin(n\pi x)$、$\lambda_n=n^2\pi^2$，即 $$G(x,\xi)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{2\sin(n\pi x)\sin(n\pi\xi)}{n^2\pi^2},$$ 与第 1 步的分段公式是同一个函数。对 $-\Delta$ 配 Dirichlet 条件还有 $G\ge0$：固定 $\xi$ 时 $G(\cdot,\xi)$ 在 $\Omega\setminus\{\xi\}$ 调和、边界为零，若它有负的最小值，该最小值只能在内部取得，与最小值原理矛盾（在 $\xi$ 附近 $G\to+\infty$，$n\ge2$；一维时 $G(\xi,\xi)>0$）。热方程与波动方程的时间依赖格林函数分别是热核与推迟核，形式上是把 $1/\lambda_n$ 换成 $e^{-\lambda_na^2t}$ 或 $\sin(a\sqrt{\lambda_n}t)/(a\sqrt{\lambda_n})$。
en: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded with smooth boundary, and consider $-\Delta$ with homogeneous Dirichlet conditions. The Green's function $G(x,\xi)$ is defined in the distributional sense by $$\begin{aligned}-\Delta_xG(x,\xi)&=\delta(x-\xi),\qquad x\in\Omega,\\ G(x,\xi)&=0,\qquad x\in\partial\Omega.\end{aligned}$$ Equivalently, for every test function $\eta$, $\int_\Omega G(x,\xi)(-\Delta\eta(x))dx=\eta(\xi)$. On $\Omega\setminus\{\xi\}$, $G$ is harmonic; at $x=\xi$ it has the singularity of the fundamental solution, appearing as a derivative jump in one dimension and as unit flux of $-\nabla G$ through a small sphere around $\xi$ in higher dimensions. On $(0,1)$ one solves directly: $$G(x,\xi)=\begin{cases}x(1-\xi),&0\le x\le\xi,\\ \xi(1-x),&\xi\le x\le1.\end{cases}$$ It is continuous at $x=\xi$ with peak $\xi(1-\xi)$; the left and right slopes are $1-\xi$ and $-\xi$, so $G'(\xi^+)-G'(\xi^-)=-1$, exactly matching $-G''=\delta$.

Representation formula. Let $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^1(\bar\Omega)$ solve $-\Delta u=f$ with $u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$. Apply Green's second identity to $u$ and $G(\cdot,\xi)$ on $\Omega\setminus B_\varepsilon(\xi)$, then let $\varepsilon\to0$ (the inner boundary $\partial B_\varepsilon(\xi)$ contributes $-u(\xi)$ in the limit, while the outer boundary is $\partial\Omega$): $$\begin{aligned}\int_\Omega&(u\Delta G-G\Delta u)\,dx\\&=\int_{\partial\Omega}\left(u\frac{\partial G}{\partial n}-G\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}\right)dS.\end{aligned}$$ Substituting $\Delta G=-\delta_\xi$ and $\Delta u=-f$, the left side is $-u(\xi)+\int_\Omega Gf$; since $G|_{\partial\Omega}=0$, the right side is $\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,\partial_nG\,dS$. Hence $$\begin{aligned}u(\xi)&=\int_\Omega G(x,\xi)f(x)\,dx\\&\quad-\int_{\partial\Omega}g(x)\frac{\partial G}{\partial n_x}(x,\xi)\,dS_x.\end{aligned}$$ For $g=0$ this is $u(\xi)=\int_\Omega Gf$: $f$ is a continuous superposition of point sources and $G$ is the response to a unit source. Here $\partial_n$ is the outward normal derivative; changing the normal convention or writing $\Delta$ instead of $-\Delta$ changes the sign of the boundary term.

Symmetry. For fixed $x,\xi$, apply Green's second identity to $G(\cdot,x)$ and $G(\cdot,\xi)$. Both vanish on the boundary, so the boundary term disappears; since $-\Delta G(\cdot,x)=\delta_x$ and $-\Delta G(\cdot,\xi)=\delta_\xi$, $$0=\int_\Omega\big[G(\eta,x)\Delta G(\eta,\xi)-G(\eta,\xi)\Delta G(\eta,x)\big]d\eta=-G(\xi,x)+G(x,\xi).$$ Therefore $G(x,\xi)=G(\xi,x)$: interchanging source and observation point leaves the response unchanged. This follows directly from self-adjointness of the operator together with the same self-adjoint boundary conditions at both ends. If the operator contains first-order terms or the boundary conditions are not self-adjoint, one must generally use the Green's function of the adjoint problem, and symmetry need not hold.

Fundamental solutions and sign conventions. In free space, the fundamental solution of $-\Delta\Phi=\delta$ is $$\Phi(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{(n-2)\sigma_n}|x|^{2-n},&n\ge3,\\[2mm] -\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\log|x|=\dfrac{1}{2\pi}\log\dfrac{1}{|x|},&n=2,\\[2mm] -\dfrac{|x|}{2},&n=1,\end{cases}$$ where $\sigma_n$ is the area of the unit sphere ($\sigma_3=4\pi$). In three dimensions this is $\Phi=1/(4\pi|x|)$; in two dimensions it is often written $\frac1{2\pi}\log\frac1{|x|}$. If the equation is instead normalized as $\Delta\Phi=\delta$, then in two dimensions one must use $+\frac1{2\pi}\log|x|$, and in three dimensions $-\frac1{4\pi|x|}$. The sign is convention-dependent, and the two-dimensional logarithm is especially error-prone. Adding any harmonic function to a fundamental solution gives another fundamental solution of the same equation; boundary conditions are what select the Green's function.

Construction on a bounded domain. Set $G(x,\xi)=\Phi(x-\xi)-h(x,\xi)$, where $h(\cdot,\xi)$ is harmonic in $\Omega$ and takes the boundary values of $\Phi(x-\xi)$. Then $-\Delta G=\delta_\xi$ and $G|_{\partial\Omega}=0$. For the ball $B_R(0)\subset\mathbb R^3$ with $\xi\ne0$, the method of images uses $\xi^*=R^2\xi/|\xi|^2$ and gives $$G(x,\xi)=\frac{1}{4\pi}\left[\frac{1}{|x-\xi|}-\frac{R}{|\xi|\,|x-\xi^*|}\right].$$ When $|x|=R$, $|x-\xi^*|=\frac{R}{|\xi|}|x-\xi|$, so the second term cancels the first and $G=0$; the formula is also symmetric. General domains have no elementary closed form; one must solve a Dirichlet problem for $h$. If the boundary is only Lipschitz, the existence and estimates for $G$ require more care. The homogeneous Neumann case $\partial_nG=0$ cannot be defined this way: $-\Delta$ has the zero eigenvalue on constants, and $\delta$ does not satisfy $\int_\Omega f=0$, so one must remove the constant mode and solve $-\Delta G=\delta-\frac1{|\Omega|}$ instead; for a general right-hand side, a solution exists only when $\int_\Omega f=0$, and $G$ is defined only up to an additive constant (a modified Green's function).

Eigenfunction expansion and positivity. Let $\{(\lambda_n,\varphi_n)\}$ be an orthonormal Dirichlet eigenbasis for $-\Delta$, with $\lambda_n>0$. Then $$G(x,\xi)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{\varphi_n(x)\varphi_n(\xi)}{\lambda_n}.$$ Applying $-\Delta_x$ termwise in the distributional sense gives $\sum\varphi_n(x)\varphi_n(\xi)=\delta(x-\xi)$, and the boundary conditions hold termwise. On $(0,1)$, $\varphi_n=\sqrt2\sin(n\pi x)$ and $\lambda_n=n^2\pi^2$, so $$G(x,\xi)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{2\sin(n\pi x)\sin(n\pi\xi)}{n^2\pi^2},$$ the same function as the piecewise formula in Step 1. For $-\Delta$ with Dirichlet conditions one also has $G\ge0$: for fixed $\xi$, $G(\cdot,\xi)$ is harmonic on $\Omega\setminus\{\xi\}$ and vanishes on the boundary; a negative minimum would have to occur in the interior, contradicting the minimum principle (near $\xi$, $G\to+\infty$ for $n\ge2$, while $G(\xi,\xi)>0$ in one dimension). The time-dependent Green's functions for the heat and wave equations are the heat kernel and the retarded kernel; formally they replace $1/\lambda_n$ by $e^{-\lambda_na^2t}$ or $\sin(a\sqrt{\lambda_n}t)/(a\sqrt{\lambda_n})$.

zh: 设 $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ 有界、连通、边界光滑（或分片光滑），$\mathbf n$ 为外单位法向，$\partial_n=\mathbf n\cdot\nabla$。我们统一用算子 $-\Delta$，考虑泊松方程 $$-\Delta u=f\ \text{于}\ \Omega.$$ 狄利克雷问题给边值 $$u=g\ \text{于}\ \partial\Omega;$$ 诺伊曼问题给法向导数 $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=g\ \text{于}\ \partial\Omega.$$ 古典解要求 $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^0(\bar\Omega)$（诺伊曼问题还需 $\nabla u$ 连续到边界）。$f=0$ 时是拉普拉斯方程。若把方程写成 $\Delta u=f$，下面由方程推出的符号关系（尤其是诺伊曼相容条件）都要相应改变；先固定 $-\Delta$ 的约定可以避免混用。

狄利克雷唯一性。设 $u_1,u_2$ 是同一 $f,g$ 的两个解，令 $w=u_1-u_2$。则 $-\Delta w=0$ 于 $\Omega$、$w=0$ 于 $\partial\Omega$。由弱最大值原理，$$\max_{ ar\Omega}w=\max_{\partial\Omega}w=0,\qquad \min_{ ar\Omega}w=\min_{\partial\Omega}w=0,$$ 故 $w\equiv0$。也可用能量法：$$ egin{aligned}0&=\int_\Omega w(-\Delta w)\,dx\&=\int_\Omega|
abla w|^2dx-\int_{\partial\Omega}w rac{\partial w}{\partial n}dS=\int_\Omega|
abla w|^2dx,\end{aligned}$$ 故 $
abla w=0$；$\Omega$ 连通且 $w|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ 给出 $w\equiv0$。两种论证都要求 $w$ 足够光滑；对弱解，用 $H^1_0$ 与 Poincaré 不等式代替。

狄利克雷的存在性与稳定性。存在性不是仅由方程自动得到的：对光滑边界与连续边值 $g$，Perron 方法（或 Green 函数表示）给出调和解；若进一步 $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$、$g\in C^{2,\alpha}(\partial\Omega)$，则解属于 $C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$。若边界有尖点或非正则点，需要屏障函数与 Wiener 判据，存在性可能失败，但唯一性不受影响。稳定性由最大值原理给出：若 $-\Delta u=0$，则 $$|u(x)|\le\max_{\partial\Omega}|g|;$$ 对一般的 $-\Delta u=f$，用比较原理配合屏障函数可得 $$\sup_\Omega|u|\le\max_{\partial\Omega}|g|+C\max_\Omega|f|,$$ 常数 $C$ 只依赖 $\Omega$ 的直径与维数。因此狄利克雷问题在 sup 范数下是适定的（在所述光滑性假设下）。

诺伊曼相容性。若 $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^1(\bar\Omega)$ 解 $-\Delta u=f$、$\partial_nu=g$，对 $-\Delta u=f$ 在 $\Omega$ 上积分并用散度定理：$$\begin{aligned}\int_\Omega f\,dx&=-\int_\Omega\Delta u\,dx\\&=-\int_{\partial\Omega}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}dS=-\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,dS.\end{aligned}$$ 因此必要条件为 $$\int_\Omega f\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,dS=0.$$ 对拉普拉斯方程 $f=0$，就是 $\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,dS=0$：稳态下净热流必须为零。若把方程写成 $\Delta u=f$，条件变成 $\int_\Omega f=\int_{\partial\Omega}g$；符号完全取决于方程与法向的约定。

诺伊曼解不唯一；相容时解集是 $u_0+C$。若 $u$ 是解，则 $u+C$ 也满足 $-\Delta(u+C)=-\Delta u$ 与 $\partial_n(u+C)=\partial_nu$。反之，若 $u_1,u_2$ 都是解，$w=u_1-u_2$ 满足 $-\Delta w=0$、$\partial_nw=0$。能量恒等式给 $$0=\int_\Omega w(-\Delta w)=\int_\Omega|
abla w|^2-\int_{\partial\Omega}w\partial_nw=\int_\Omega|
abla w|^2,$$ 故 $
abla w=0$；$\Omega$ 连通，$w\equiv C$。因此解在相差一个常数的意义下唯一；要唯一确定，可加规范化 $\int_\Omega u\,dx=0$。相容性条件在适当光滑性下也是充分的（例如用弱解与 Fredholm 二择一，或对 $-\Delta$ 的诺伊曼级数），并非只是必要条件。

例子与混合边界。一维 $-u''=1$ 于 $(0,1)$、$u'(0)=u'(1)=0$：相容性给 $\int_0^1 1\,dx+(-u'(0))+u'(1)=1
e0$，故无解；直接积分也得 $-u'(1)+u'(0)=1$，与 $0=1$ 矛盾。若改成 $u'(0)=0$、$u'(1)=-1$，则 $u=-x^2/2+C$ 是解，$C$ 任意，正体现诺伊曼问题的常数自由度。混合边界（边界一部分给 Dirichlet、其余给 Neumann）通常恢复唯一性：若 $w$ 调和、在 Dirichlet 部分为零、在 Neumann 部分法向导数为零，能量恒等式仍给 $\int|

en: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded, connected, with smooth (or piecewise smooth) boundary, and let $\mathbf n$ denote the outward unit normal, with $\partial_n=\mathbf n\cdot\nabla$. We consistently use the operator $-\Delta$ and consider the Poisson equation $$-\Delta u=f\ \text{in}\ \Omega.$$ The Dirichlet problem prescribes boundary values $$u=g\ \text{on}\ \partial\Omega;$$ the Neumann problem prescribes the normal derivative $$\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=g\ \text{on}\ \partial\Omega.$$ A classical solution requires $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^0(\bar\Omega)$ (and, for Neumann, $\nabla u$ continuous up to the boundary). When $f=0$ this is Laplace's equation. If the equation is written as $\Delta u=f$, the sign relations derived below (especially the Neumann compatibility condition) must be changed accordingly; fixing the $-\Delta$ convention first prevents confusion.

Uniqueness for Dirichlet. Let $u_1,u_2$ solve the same problem with data $f,g$, and set $w=u_1-u_2$. Then $-\Delta w=0$ in $\Omega$ and $w=0$ on $\partial\Omega$. The weak maximum principle gives $$\max_{ ar\Omega}w=\max_{\partial\Omega}w=0,\qquad \min_{ ar\Omega}w=\min_{\partial\Omega}w=0,$$ hence $w\equiv0$. An energy proof is also available: $$ egin{aligned}0&=\int_\Omega w(-\Delta w)\,dx\&=\int_\Omega|
abla w|^2dx-\int_{\partial\Omega}w rac{\partial w}{\partial n}dS=\int_\Omega|
abla w|^2dx,\end{aligned}$$ so $
abla w=0$; since $\Omega$ is connected and $w|_{\partial\Omega}=0$, $w\equiv0$. Both arguments require sufficient smoothness; for weak solutions, use $H^1_0$ and the Poincaré inequality instead.

Existence and stability for Dirichlet. Existence does not follow from the equation alone: for smooth boundary and continuous boundary data $g$, the Perron method (or the Green's function representation) produces a harmonic solution; if moreover $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ and $g\in C^{2,\alpha}(\partial\Omega)$, the solution belongs to $C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$. If the boundary has corners or nonregular points, barrier functions and the Wiener criterion are needed, and existence may fail, although uniqueness is unaffected. Stability follows from the maximum principle: if $-\Delta u=0$, then $$|u(x)|\le\max_{\partial\Omega}|g|;$$ for general $-\Delta u=f$, comparison with a barrier function gives $$\sup_\Omega|u|\le\max_{\partial\Omega}|g|+C\max_\Omega|f|,$$ where $C$ depends only on the diameter and dimension of $\Omega$. Thus the Dirichlet problem is well posed in the sup norm under the stated smoothness hypotheses.

Neumann compatibility. If $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^1(\bar\Omega)$ solves $-\Delta u=f$ with $\partial_nu=g$, integrate $-\Delta u=f$ over $\Omega$ and use the divergence theorem: $$\begin{aligned}\int_\Omega f\,dx&=-\int_\Omega\Delta u\,dx\\&=-\int_{\partial\Omega}\frac{\partial u}{\partial n}dS=-\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,dS.\end{aligned}$$ Hence the necessary condition is $$\int_\Omega f\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,dS=0.$$ For Laplace's equation $f=0$ this becomes $\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,dS=0$: in a steady state the net heat flux must vanish. If the equation is written as $\Delta u=f$, the condition becomes $\int_\Omega f=\int_{\partial\Omega}g$; the sign depends entirely on the sign convention for the equation and the normal.

Nonuniqueness for Neumann; when compatible, the solution set is $u_0+C$. If $u$ solves the problem, then $u+C$ satisfies $-\Delta(u+C)=-\Delta u$ and $\partial_n(u+C)=\partial_nu$. Conversely, if $u_1,u_2$ are two solutions, $w=u_1-u_2$ satisfies $-\Delta w=0$ and $\partial_nw=0$. The energy identity gives $$0=\int_\Omega w(-\Delta w)=\int_\Omega|
abla w|^2-\int_{\partial\Omega}w\partial_nw=\int_\Omega|
abla w|^2,$$ so $
abla w=0$; since $\Omega$ is connected, $w\equiv C$. Thus solutions are unique only up to an additive constant; uniqueness can be restored by the normalization $\int_\Omega u\,dx=0$. Under suitable smoothness, the compatibility condition is also sufficient (for example via weak solutions and the Fredholm alternative, or a Neumann series for $-\Delta$), not merely necessary.

An example and mixed boundary conditions. In one dimension, $-u''=1$ on $(0,1)$ with $u'(0)=u'(1)=0$ has no solution: compatibility gives $\int_0^1 1\,dx+(-u'(0))+u'(1)=1
e0$, and direct integration gives $-u'(1)+u'(0)=1$, contradicting $0=1$. If instead $u'(0)=0$ and $u'(1)=-1$, then $u=-x^2/2+C$ solves the problem for arbitrary $C$, exhibiting the constant freedom of the Neumann problem. Mixed boundary conditions (Dirichlet on part of the boundary, Neumann on the rest) usually restore uniqueness: if $w$ is harmonic, vanishes on the Dirichlet part, and has zero normal derivative on the Neumann part, the energy identity still gives $\int|
abla w|^2=0$, so $w$ is constant and the Dirichlet part forces $w\equiv0$. Only the pure Neumann problem (with $\Omega$ connected) retains a one-constant family; Robin conditions are also unique, for example when $ eta
e0$, $\alpha/ eta\ge0$, and $\alpha
e0$. The conclusions for the Poisson and Laplace equations are the same; only the presence of $f$ and the existence estimates differ.

zh: 设 $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ 有界、连通，$c\in C(\bar\Omega)$ 且 $c\le0$。定义椭圆算子 $$Lu=\Delta u+cu.$$ 弱最大值原理：若 $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^0(\bar\Omega)$ 满足 $Lu\ge0$ 于 $\Omega$，则 $$\max_{\bar\Omega}u\le\max_{\partial\Omega}u^+,\qquad u^+=\max(u,0).$$ 特别地，若 $u\le0$ 于 $\partial\Omega$，则 $u\le0$ 于 $\Omega$。条件 $c\le0$ 的符号来源是：若 $u$ 在内部取到正的最大值 $M>0$，则在该点 $\Delta u\le0$ 且 $cu=cM\le0$，于是 $Lu\le0$；这与 $Lu\ge0$ 只能在 $Lu=0$ 时相容，而要排除内部正极大还需强形式或扰动论证。若改用 $-\Delta+c$，主部符号相反，$c$ 的条件与不等式方向必须相应改写：例如对 $L'=-\Delta+c$，取 $c\ge0$ 时应把 $L'u\ge0$ 改为 $L'u\le0$；不能把这里的 $c\le0$ 直接照搬。

弱形式的证明（扰动法）。取 $\alpha>0$ 使 $\alpha^2>\|c\|_\infty$，令 $$v(x)=u(x)+\varepsilon e^{\alpha x_1},\qquad \varepsilon>0.$$ 则 $$Lv=Lu+\varepsilon e^{\alpha x_1}(\alpha^2+c)\ge\varepsilon e^{\alpha x_1}(\alpha^2-\|c\|_\infty)>0.$$ 若 $v$ 在内部某点取到非负最大值，则在该点 $\Delta v\le0$、$cv\le0$，故 $Lv\le0$，矛盾。若 $\max_{\bar\Omega}v<0$，则 $u<0$ 处处，结论平凡；否则 $\max v\ge0$，它不能在内部取得，故在边界取得，且对任意 $x$，$$\begin{aligned}u(x)&\le v(x)\le\max_{\partial\Omega}v\\&\le\max_{\partial\Omega}u^++\varepsilon\max_{\partial\Omega}e^{\alpha x_1}.\end{aligned}$$ 令 $\varepsilon\to0$ 得 $\max_{\bar\Omega}u\le\max_{\partial\Omega}u^+$。

强最大值原理与 Hopf 引理。在同样 $c\le0$、$Lu\ge0$ 下，若 $u$ 在 $\Omega$ 的内点取到非负最大值，则 $u$ 在 $\Omega$ 内恒为常数。证明可用 Hopf 引理或平均值公式；关键是内部正极大处 $Lu=0$ 会迫使 $\Delta u=0$ 且 $cu=0$，再沿任意小球用平均值性质传播。对 $c=0$ 的调和函数，非负限制可以去掉：非常数调和函数在内部既不能取极大也不能取极小。Hopf 引理还给出边界形式：若 $u$ 在边界点取严格最大值，则外法向导数 $\partial_nu>0$（在边界光滑、$u$ 足够光滑时）。$c>0$ 时结论失效：在 $(0,\pi)$ 上 $u=\sin x$、$c=1$，$Lu=-\sin x+\sin x=0$，但 $u$ 在 $\pi/2$ 取正极大而不为常数。

比较原理与狄利克雷唯一性。若 $Lu\ge Lv$ 于 $\Omega$、$u\le v$ 于 $\partial\Omega$，令 $w=u-v$，则 $Lw\ge0$、$w\le0$ 于边界，弱最大值原理给 $w\le0$，即 $u\le v$。取 $u,v$ 为 $Lu=f$、$u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$ 的两个解，$w$ 满足 $Lw=0$、$w=0$ 于边界；对 $w$ 和 $-w$ 分别用弱最大值原理，得 $w\le0$ 与 $-w\le0$，故 $w=0$。因此 $Lu=f$、$u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$ 的古典解至多一个。若 $c\le0$ 改为 $c>0$，唯一性可能失效：例如 $w''+cw=0$ 在 $(0,\pi)$、$w(0)=w(\pi)=0$，当 $c=1$ 时有非零解 $\sin x$。

抛物型最大值原理。设 $Q=\Omega\times(0,T]$，抛物边界 $$\Gamma_T=(\Omega\times\{0\})\cup(\partial\Omega\times[0,T]).$$ 记 $Pu=u_t-a^2\Delta u$（一维为 $u_t-a^2u_{xx}$）。设 $u\in C^2(Q)\cap C^0(\bar Q)$；若 $Pu\le0$ 于 $Q$，则 $$\max_{\bar Q}u=\max_{\Gamma_T}u.$$ 证明要点：若最大值在 $0<t_0<T$、$x_0\in\Omega$ 取得，则 $u_t(x_0,t_0)=0$、$\Delta u(x_0,t_0)\le0$，故 $Pu\ge0$；与 $Pu\le0$ 合起来只能 $Pu=0$，再由强最大值原理迫使 $u$ 为常数，最大值仍在抛物边界。落在 $t=T$ 的退化情形可对 $u-\varepsilon t$ 作扰动排除。注意不等式方向与椭圆情形相反：椭圆 $Lu\ge0$ 把最大值推到边界，抛物型 $Pu\le0$ 才把最大值推到抛物边界；这是由 $P$ 中 $-a^2\Delta$ 与 $\partial_t$ 的符号共同决定的。

应用与边界。对热方程 $u_t=a^2u_{xx}$、齐次 Dirichlet 边界、初值 $\varphi$，抛物型最大值原理给 $$|u(x,t)|\le\max_{[0,L]}|\varphi|,$$ 因为 $u$ 与 $-u$ 都满足 $Pu=0$；这同时给出唯一性与对初值的连续依赖，初值误差不会随时间放大。比较原理也成立：若两个解在抛物边界上有序，则在内部有序。反向热方程 $u_t=-a^2u_{xx}$ 可写成 $Qu=u_t+a^2u_{xx}=0$；在内部极大处 $u_t=0$、$u_{xx}\le0$，故 $Qu\le0$，与正向算子 $P=\partial_t-a^2\Delta$ 在内部极大处 $Pu\ge0$ 的符号相反。更根本的是，最大值原理依赖空间主部 $-a^2\Delta$ 的负定性；反向方程的空间主部是 $+a^2\Delta$，在内部极大处不再产生矛盾，故最大值原理失效。等价地，高频模式 $e^{a^2\lambda_nt}$ 指数增长，反向问题是不适定的。最后，椭圆情形的结论依赖 $\Omega$ 有界、$u$ 连续到边界、$c\le0$；抛物型则要求 $Q$ 有界且 $u$ 连续到抛物边界。在无界区域上 $u(x,y)=x$ 在 $\{x>0\}$ 内调和、边界为零但无上界；$c>0$ 的反例已在第 3 步给出。Neumann/Robin 边界需用 Hopf 引理处理边界极值。
en: Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be bounded and connected, and let $c\in C(\bar\Omega)$ with $c\le0$. Define the elliptic operator $$Lu=\Delta u+cu.$$ The weak maximum principle states: if $u\in C^2(\Omega)\cap C^0(\bar\Omega)$ and $Lu\ge0$ in $\Omega$, then $$\max_{\bar\Omega}u\le\max_{\partial\Omega}u^+,\qquad u^+=\max(u,0).$$ In particular, if $u\le0$ on $\partial\Omega$, then $u\le0$ in $\Omega$. The sign condition $c\le0$ comes from the following observation: if $u$ has a positive interior maximum $M>0$, then at that point $\Delta u\le0$ and $cu=cM\le0$, so $Lu\le0$; this is compatible with $Lu\ge0$ only when $Lu=0$, and excluding such an interior positive maximum still requires the strong form or a perturbation argument. If the operator is instead written $-\Delta+c$, the principal part has the opposite sign, so the sign condition on $c$ and the inequality direction must both be reformulated: for instance, for $L'=-\Delta+c$ with $c\ge0$, one should replace $L'u\ge0$ by $L'u\le0$. The condition $c\le0$ here cannot be transferred verbatim.

Proof of the weak form (perturbation). Choose $\alpha>0$ with $\alpha^2>\|c\|_\infty$ and set $$v(x)=u(x)+\varepsilon e^{\alpha x_1},\qquad \varepsilon>0.$$ Then $$Lv=Lu+\varepsilon e^{\alpha x_1}(\alpha^2+c)\ge\varepsilon e^{\alpha x_1}(\alpha^2-\|c\|_\infty)>0.$$ If $v$ attained a nonnegative maximum at an interior point, then at that point $\Delta v\le0$ and $cv\le0$, so $Lv\le0$, a contradiction. If $\max_{\bar\Omega}v<0$, then $u<0$ everywhere and the conclusion is trivial. Otherwise $\max v\ge0$, so it is attained on the boundary, and for every $x$, $$\begin{aligned}u(x)&\le v(x)\le\max_{\partial\Omega}v\\&\le\max_{\partial\Omega}u^++\varepsilon\max_{\partial\Omega}e^{\alpha x_1}.\end{aligned}$$ Letting $\varepsilon\to0$ gives $\max_{\bar\Omega}u\le\max_{\partial\Omega}u^+$.

The strong maximum principle and Hopf's lemma. Under the same assumptions $c\le0$, $Lu\ge0$, if $u$ attains a nonnegative maximum at an interior point of $\Omega$, then $u$ is constant throughout $\Omega$. This can be proved via Hopf's lemma or the mean value formula; the key point is that at an interior positive maximum, $Lu=0$ forces $\Delta u=0$ and $cu=0$, and the mean value property propagates constancy over arbitrary small balls. For a harmonic function ($c=0$), the nonnegativity restriction can be dropped: a nonconstant harmonic function has neither an interior maximum nor an interior minimum. Hopf's lemma also gives a boundary form: if $u$ has a strict maximum at a boundary point, then the outward normal derivative satisfies $\partial_nu>0$ (for smooth boundary and sufficient smoothness of $u$). The condition $c\le0$ cannot be dropped: on $(0,\pi)$, $u=\sin x$ with $c=1$ satisfies $Lu=-\sin x+\sin x=0$, yet $u$ has a positive interior maximum at $\pi/2$ and is not constant.

Comparison principle and Dirichlet uniqueness. If $Lu\ge Lv$ in $\Omega$ and $u\le v$ on $\partial\Omega$, set $w=u-v$. Then $Lw\ge0$ and $w\le0$ on the boundary, so the weak maximum principle gives $w\le0$, i.e. $u\le v$. Now take two solutions $u,v$ of $Lu=f$ with $u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$; then $w=u-v$ satisfies $Lw=0$ and $w=0$ on the boundary. Applying the weak maximum principle to $w$ and to $-w$ gives $w\le0$ and $-w\le0$, hence $w=0$. Therefore the classical solution of $Lu=f$, $u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$ is unique. If $c\le0$ is replaced by $c>0$, uniqueness may fail: for example, $w''+cw=0$ on $(0,\pi)$ with $w(0)=w(\pi)=0$ has the nonzero solution $\sin x$ when $c=1$.

The parabolic maximum principle. Let $Q=\Omega\times(0,T]$ and define the parabolic boundary $$\Gamma_T=(\Omega\times\{0\})\cup(\partial\Omega\times[0,T]).$$ Write $Pu=u_t-a^2\Delta u$ (in one dimension, $u_t-a^2u_{xx}$). Let $u\in C^2(Q)\cap C^0(\bar Q)$; if $Pu\le0$ in $Q$, then $$\max_{\bar Q}u=\max_{\Gamma_T}u.$$ Sketch: if the maximum occurs at $0<t_0<T$, $x_0\in\Omega$, then $u_t(x_0,t_0)=0$ and $\Delta u(x_0,t_0)\le0$, so $Pu\ge0$; together with $Pu\le0$ this forces $Pu=0$, and the strong maximum principle then makes $u$ constant, so the maximum is still on the parabolic boundary. The degenerate case where the maximum occurs at $t=T$ is excluded by applying the argument to $u-\varepsilon t$. Note that the inequality direction is opposite to the elliptic case: for $L$, $Lu\ge0$ pushes the maximum to the boundary, while for $P$, $Pu\le0$ pushes it to the parabolic boundary. This is due to the signs of $-a^2\Delta$ and $\partial_t$ in $P$.

Applications and limitations. For the heat equation $u_t=a^2u_{xx}$ with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary and initial data $\varphi$, the parabolic maximum principle gives $$|u(x,t)|\le\max_{[0,L]}|\varphi|,$$ since both $u$ and $-u$ satisfy $Pu=0$. This yields uniqueness and continuous dependence on the initial data; initial errors never grow in time. A comparison principle also holds: if two solutions are ordered on the parabolic boundary, they are ordered in the interior. The backward heat equation $u_t=-a^2u_{xx}$ can be written as $Qu=u_t+a^2u_{xx}=0$; at an interior maximum $u_t=0$ and $u_{xx}\le0$, so $Qu\le0$, the opposite of the sign $Pu\ge0$ for the forward operator $P=\partial_t-a^2\Delta$ at an interior maximum. More fundamentally, the maximum principle relies on the negative definiteness of the spatial principal part $-a^2\Delta$; for the backward equation the spatial principal part is $+a^2\Delta$, so no contradiction arises at an interior maximum and the maximum principle fails. Equivalently, high-frequency modes $e^{a^2\lambda_nt}$ grow exponentially, and the backward problem is ill posed. Finally, the elliptic conclusions require $\Omega$ bounded, $u$ continuous up to the boundary, and $c\le0$; the parabolic version requires $Q$ bounded and $u$ continuous up to the parabolic boundary. On the unbounded domain $\{x>0\}$, the harmonic function $u(x,y)=x$ has zero boundary data but is unbounded above; the counterexample for $c>0$ was given in Step 3. Neumann or Robin boundary conditions require Hopf's lemma to handle boundary extrema.

zh: 设数据空间 $X$、解空间 $Y$，定解问题定义一个解映射 $S:X\to Y$。称问题在 Hadamard 意义下适定，若同时满足：(1) 存在性：对每个 $d\in X$，存在解 $u=S(d)\in Y$；(2) 唯一性：这样的解只有一个；(3) 连续依赖（稳定性）：$S$ 连续，即存在常数 $C$ 使 $$\|S(d)\|_Y\le C\|d\|_X$$（线性问题），或对 $d_n\to d$ 有 $S(d_n)\to S(d)$（非线性问题）。三个条件必须在明确的范数与数据类下陈述；只证明存在，或只证明存在与唯一，而不给出稳定性估计，都不足以称为适定。反过来，稳定性也离不开存在性：没有解就谈不上解映射连续。

波动方程的能量法。考虑 $u_{tt}=a^2u_{xx}$（$0<x<L$）、$u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0$，初值 $u(x,0)=\varphi$、$u_t(x,0)=\psi$。对古典解定义 $$E(t)=\frac12\int_0^L\left(u_t^2+a^2u_x^2\right)dx.$$ 则 $$\begin{aligned}\frac{dE}{dt}&=\int_0^L(u_tu_{tt}+a^2u_xu_{xt})dx\\&=a^2\int_0^L(u_tu_{xx}+u_xu_{xt})dx\\&=a^2\big[u_tu_x\big]_0^L=0,\end{aligned}$$ 最后一步用了 $u_t(0,t)=u_t(L,t)=0$（由边界条件对 $t$ 求导）。故 $E(t)=E(0)$。若两个解之差 $w$ 有零初值，则 $E_w(0)=0$，从而 $w_t=w_x=0$，$w$ 为常数；零初值给 $w=0$，唯一性成立。对一般解，$$E(t)=E(0)=\frac12\int_0^L\left(\psi^2+a^2\varphi'^2\right)dx,$$ 给出能量范数下的连续依赖。存在性：$\varphi\in H^1_0$、$\psi\in L^2$ 时用 Galerkin 或傅里叶级数构造弱解；数据光滑且相容时由达朗贝尔公式或级数给出古典解。

热方程的最大值原理。考虑 $u_t=a^2u_{xx}$（$0<x<L$）、$u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0$、$u(x,0)=\varphi(x)$。抛物型最大值原理给 $$|u(x,t)|\le\max_{0\le x\le L}|\varphi(x)|.$$ 于是解唯一（差满足齐次方程与零初值，界为 $0$），且对初值的连续依赖是 Lipschitz 的，误差不随时间放大。存在性：对 $\varphi\in L^2$，正弦级数 $$u(x,t)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n e^{-(n\pi a/L)^2t}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}$$ 在每个 $t\ge\delta>0$ 上一致收敛且任意阶可微，并在 $L^2$ 意义下 $u(\cdot,t)\to\varphi$；若 $\varphi$ 连续且 $\varphi(0)=\varphi(L)=0$，则解连续到 $t=0$。源项用 Duhamel 原理叠加。正向热方程因此是适定的，而且有平滑效应。

拉普拉斯方程：狄利克雷问题适定，柯西问题不适定。对 $-\Delta u=0$、$u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$，最大值原理给唯一性与 $$\|u\|_\infty\le\|g\|_\infty;$$ 光滑边界与连续 $g$ 时 Perron 方法给存在性，故在 sup 范数下适定。但同一个方程配上柯西数据 $(u,\partial_nu)$ 可能不适定。上半平面 $\{y>0\}$ 上的阿达马例子 $$u_n(x,y)=\frac{1}{n^2}\sin(nx)\sinh(ny)$$ 满足 $\Delta u_n=0$；在 $y=0$ 上 $u_n=0$、$\partial_yu_n=\frac1n\sin(nx)$，两者都一致趋于 $0$；但在任意固定 $y_0>0$，$$\sup_x|u_n(x,y_0)|=\frac{\sinh(ny_0)}{n^2}\to\infty.$$ 数据任意小、解任意大，连续依赖失败，故柯西问题不适定。

三个条件缺一不可。诺伊曼问题说明存在性与唯一性可以分别失败：$-\Delta u=f$、$\partial_nu=g$ 若 $\int_\Omega f+\int_{\partial\Omega}g\ne0$ 则无解（存在性失败）；若已有解 $u$，则 $u+C$ 都是解（唯一性失败），加规范化 $\int u=0$ 后才唯一。阿达马例子说明即使每个数据都有（在解析类中唯一的）解，稳定性仍可能失败：每个 $n$ 对应的数据都有解，但数据趋零时解不趋零；柯西–柯瓦列夫斯卡娅定理在解析数据类中给出局部唯一解，却仍不能保证连续依赖。连续依赖还必须指明范数：同一个问题换用另一对范数时，结论可能改变；Hadamard 适定性是相对于固定数据类与拓扑而言的。

对不适定问题，必须引入先验信息或正则化：吉洪诺夫正则化、截断奇异值分解、Landweber 迭代、全变差正则化等；在紧集上常可恢复条件稳定性（例如对数型估计），但通常不可能在全数据空间上恢复 Lipschitz 连续依赖。数值上还要区分适定性与离散稳定性：即使连续问题适定，格式仍需满足稳定性条件（如波动方程的 CFL 条件）；线性情形下，相容加稳定等价于收敛（Lax 等价原理）。最后，适定性的三条件是一个整体：只证存在（甚至存在加唯一）而不给稳定性估计，不能称为适定；反过来，物理上不适定的反问题仍可能有用，但必须报告条件数、噪声放大与正则化参数。
en: Let $X$ be a data space and $Y$ a solution space, and let the problem define a solution map $S:X\to Y$. The problem is well posed in the sense of Hadamard if all three conditions hold: (1) existence: for every $d\in X$ there is a solution $u=S(d)\in Y$; (2) uniqueness: this solution is the only one; (3) continuous dependence (stability): $S$ is continuous, i.e. there is a constant $C$ with $$\|S(d)\|_Y\le C\|d\|_X$$ for linear problems, or $S(d_n)\to S(d)$ whenever $d_n\to d$ for nonlinear problems. All three conditions must be stated for specified norms and data classes. Proving existence alone, or existence and uniqueness without a stability estimate, is not enough to call the problem well posed. Conversely, stability presupposes existence: without a solution there is no solution map to be continuous.

Energy method for the wave equation. Consider $u_{tt}=a^2u_{xx}$ on $0<x<L$ with $u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0$ and initial data $u(x,0)=\varphi$, $u_t(x,0)=\psi$. For a classical solution define $$E(t)=\frac12\int_0^L\left(u_t^2+a^2u_x^2\right)dx.$$ Then $$\begin{aligned}\frac{dE}{dt}&=\int_0^L(u_tu_{tt}+a^2u_xu_{xt})dx\\&=a^2\int_0^L(u_tu_{xx}+u_xu_{xt})dx\\&=a^2\big[u_tu_x\big]_0^L=0,\end{aligned}$$ where the last step uses $u_t(0,t)=u_t(L,t)=0$, obtained by differentiating the boundary conditions in $t$. Hence $E(t)=E(0)$. If $w$ is the difference of two solutions with zero initial data, then $E_w(0)=0$, so $w_t=w_x=0$ and $w$ is constant; zero initial data then give $w=0$, proving uniqueness. For a general solution, $$E(t)=E(0)=\frac12\int_0^L\left(\psi^2+a^2\varphi'^2\right)dx,$$ which yields continuous dependence in the energy norm. Existence: for $\varphi\in H^1_0$ and $\psi\in L^2$, Galerkin's method or Fourier series constructs a weak solution; for smooth compatible data, d'Alembert's formula or the series gives a classical solution.

Maximum principle for the heat equation. Consider $u_t=a^2u_{xx}$ on $0<x<L$ with $u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0$ and $u(x,0)=\varphi(x)$. The parabolic maximum principle gives $$|u(x,t)|\le\max_{0\le x\le L}|\varphi(x)|.$$ Hence the solution is unique (the difference satisfies the homogeneous equation with zero initial data and has bound $0$), and continuous dependence on the initial data is Lipschitz, with errors not growing in time. Existence: for $\varphi\in L^2$, the sine series $$u(x,t)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n e^{-(n\pi a/L)^2t}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}$$ converges uniformly on every $t\ge\delta>0$ and is infinitely differentiable; moreover $u(\cdot,t)\to\varphi$ in $L^2$. If $\varphi$ is continuous and $\varphi(0)=\varphi(L)=0$, the solution is continuous up to $t=0$. Source terms are handled by Duhamel's principle. The forward heat equation is therefore well posed and has a smoothing effect.

Laplace's equation: the Dirichlet problem is well posed, but the Cauchy problem is ill posed. For $-\Delta u=0$ with $u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$, the maximum principle gives uniqueness and $$\|u\|_\infty\le\|g\|_\infty;$$ for smooth boundary and continuous $g$, the Perron method gives existence, so the problem is well posed in the sup norm. Yet the same equation with Cauchy data $(u,\partial_nu)$ can be ill posed. Hadamard's example on the upper half-plane $\{y>0\}$, $$u_n(x,y)=\frac{1}{n^2}\sin(nx)\sinh(ny),$$ satisfies $\Delta u_n=0$. On $y=0$, $u_n=0$ and $\partial_yu_n=\frac1n\sin(nx)$, both tending to $0$ uniformly; but for any fixed $y_0>0$, $$\sup_x|u_n(x,y_0)|=\frac{\sinh(ny_0)}{n^2}\to\infty.$$ The data are arbitrarily small while the solution is arbitrarily large, so continuous dependence fails and the Cauchy problem is ill posed.

All three conditions are indispensable. The Neumann problem shows that existence and uniqueness can fail separately: for $-\Delta u=f$ with $\partial_nu=g$, if $\int_\Omega f+\int_{\partial\Omega}g\ne0$ there is no solution (existence fails); if a solution $u$ exists, then every $u+C$ is a solution (uniqueness fails), and the normalization $\int u=0$ restores uniqueness. Hadamard's example shows that even when every data set has an (analytically unique) solution, stability may still fail: each $n$-th data set has a solution, but the solutions do not tend to zero as the data do. The Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem provides a locally unique solution in the analytic data class, yet continuous dependence still fails. Continuous dependence must also specify the norms: the same problem may behave differently under another pair of norms, and Hadamard well-posedness is relative to a fixed data class and topology.

For ill-posed problems one must impose prior information or regularization: Tikhonov regularization, truncated singular value decomposition, Landweber iteration, total variation regularization, and others. On compact sets one can often recover conditional stability (for example logarithmic estimates), but usually not Lipschitz continuous dependence on the whole data space. Numerically, well-posedness of the continuous problem must be distinguished from discrete stability: even a well-posed continuous problem requires a stable scheme (for example, the CFL condition for the wave equation); in the linear case, consistency plus stability is equivalent to convergence (the Lax equivalence principle). Finally, the three conditions form a single package: proving existence alone (or even existence and uniqueness) without a stability estimate does not establish well-posedness. Conversely, physically meaningful inverse problems may be ill posed, but then condition numbers, noise amplification, and regularization parameters must be reported.
